questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A block of ice of mass $150 \text{ g}$ at $0^\circ\text{C}$ is dropped into $250 \text{ g}$ of water at $T^\circ\text{C}$. It is observed that exactly $100 \text{ g}$ of ice melts by the time the mixture reaches thermal equilibrium. The value of $T$ is ________.

[Use: Specific heat capacity of water $= 4200 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, Latent heat of fusion of ice $= 3.36 \times 10^5 \text{ J kg}^{-1}$]
questions.question:
A block of ice of mass $150 \text{ g}$ at $0^\circ\text{C}$ is dropped into $250 \text{ g}$ of water at $T^\circ\text{C}$. It is observed that exactly $100 \text{ g}$ of ice melts by the time the mixture reaches thermal equilibrium. The value of $T$ is ________.

[Use: Specific heat capacity of water $= 4200 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, Latent heat of fusion of ice $= 3.36 \times 10^5 \text{ J kg}^{-1}$]
questions.solution:
Since only a part of the ice melts ($100 \text{ g}$ out of $150 \text{ g}$), the final temperature of the mixture must be $0^\circ\text{C}$.

According to the principle of calorimetry, the heat lost by the water equals the heat gained by the melting ice.

Heat lost by water:
$\Delta Q_1 = m_w s_w \Delta T$
$\Delta Q_1 = 0.25 \times 4200 \times (T - 0) = 1050 T \text{ J}$

Heat gained by ice to melt $100 \text{ g}$:
$\Delta Q_2 = m_{\text{melt}} L$
$\Delta Q_2 = 0.1 \times 3.36 \times 10^5 = 33600 \text{ J}$

Equating the heat lost and heat gained:
$1050 T = 33600$
$T = \dfrac{33600}{1050} = 32$

The initial temperature of the water was $32^\circ\text{C}$.

Answer: $32$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two solid cylindrical rods 1 and 2 of different materials are joined end-to-end in series. The free end of rod 1 is maintained at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ and the free end of rod 2 is kept at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$. In the steady state, the temperature of the interface between the two rods is $80^{\circ}\text{C}$. If the ratio of their lengths is $\dfrac{L_1}{L_2} = 2$ and the ratio of their radii is $\dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = 2$, then the ratio of their thermal conductivities $\dfrac{K_1}{K_2}$ is ________.
questions.question: Two solid cylindrical rods 1 and 2 of different materials are joined end-to-end in series. The free end of rod 1 is maintained at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ and the free end of rod 2 is kept at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$. In the steady state, the temperature of the interface between the two rods is $80^{\circ}\text{C}$. If the ratio of their lengths is $\dfrac{L_1}{L_2} = 2$ and the ratio of their radii is $\dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = 2$, then the ratio of their thermal conductivities $\dfrac{K_1}{K_2}$ is ________.
questions.solution:
Let the thermal resistances of rod 1 and rod 2 be $R_1$ and $R_2$ respectively.

In steady state, the rate of heat flow through both rods is the same:
$\dfrac{100 - 80}{R_1} = \dfrac{80 - 0}{R_2}$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{20}{R_1} = \dfrac{80}{R_2} \Rightarrow \dfrac{R_2}{R_1} = 4$

The thermal resistance of a cylindrical rod is given by $R = \dfrac{L}{K \pi r^2}$.

Therefore, the ratio of their resistances is:
$\dfrac{R_2}{R_1} = \left(\dfrac{L_2}{L_1}\right) \left(\dfrac{K_1}{K_2}\right) \left(\dfrac{r_1}{r_2}\right)^2$

Given $\dfrac{L_1}{L_2} = 2 \Rightarrow \dfrac{L_2}{L_1} = \dfrac{1}{2}$ and $\dfrac{r_1}{r_2} = 2$.

Substituting these values:
$4 = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \left(\dfrac{K_1}{K_2}\right) (2)^2$

$4 = \left(\dfrac{1}{2}\right) \left(\dfrac{K_1}{K_2}\right) (4)$

$4 = 2 \left(\dfrac{K_1}{K_2}\right)$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{K_1}{K_2} = 2$

Answer: $2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal rod of length $5.0 \text{ m}$ and mass $200 \text{ g}$ is supplied with $4000 \text{ J}$ of heat energy. The specific heat capacity of the metal is $500 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ and its coefficient of linear expansion is $1.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ K}^{-1}$. Assuming no heat is lost to the surroundings, what is the increase in the length of the rod?
questions.question: A metal rod of length $5.0 \text{ m}$ and mass $200 \text{ g}$ is supplied with $4000 \text{ J}$ of heat energy. The specific heat capacity of the metal is $500 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$ and its coefficient of linear expansion is $1.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ K}^{-1}$. Assuming no heat is lost to the surroundings, what is the increase in the length of the rod?
questions.solution:
First, calculate the change in temperature of the rod using the calorimetry formula $Q = mc\Delta T$.

Given:
$Q = 4000 \text{ J}$
$m = 200 \text{ g} = 0.2 \text{ kg}$
$c = 500 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$

$\Delta T = \dfrac{Q}{mc} = \dfrac{4000}{0.2 \times 500} = \dfrac{4000}{100} = 40 \text{ K}$

Next, calculate the increase in length using the linear expansion formula $\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta T$.

Given:
$L_0 = 5.0 \text{ m}$
$\alpha = 1.2 \times 10^{-5} \text{ K}^{-1}$

$\Delta L = 5.0 \times 1.2 \times 10^{-5} \times 40$

$\Delta L = 240 \times 10^{-5} \text{ m} = 2.4 \times 10^{-3} \text{ m}$

Converting to millimeters:
$\Delta L = 2.4 \text{ mm}$

Answer: $2.4 \text{ mm}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rigid container initially holds nitrogen gas at standard temperature and pressure. When $415\ \text{J}$ of heat is supplied to the gas, its temperature increases by $10.0^\circ\text{C}$. The volume of the container is (Given gas constant $R=8.3\ \text{J}\ \text{K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)
questions.question: A rigid container initially holds nitrogen gas at standard temperature and pressure. When $415\ \text{J}$ of heat is supplied to the gas, its temperature increases by $10.0^\circ\text{C}$. The volume of the container is (Given gas constant $R=8.3\ \text{J}\ \text{K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
Since the container is rigid, the volume is constant, making the process isochoric.

For a diatomic gas like nitrogen ($N_2$), the molar heat capacity at constant volume is $C_v = \dfrac{5}{2}R$.

The heat supplied is given by $Q = n C_v \Delta T$. Substituting the given values:
$415 = n \left(\dfrac{5}{2} \times 8.3\right) (10)$
$415 = n \times 20.75 \times 10$
$415 = 207.5\ n$
$n = 2\ \text{mol}$

At standard temperature and pressure (STP), one mole of an ideal gas occupies $22.4\ \text{L}$.

Therefore, the volume of the container is:
$V = n \times 22.4 = 2 \times 22.4 = 44.8\ \text{L}$

Answer: $44.8\ \text{L}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid substance of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is heated uniformly by a constant power source of $500\text{ W}$. The temperature-time heating curve of the substance shows a solid heating phase, a melting plateau, and a liquid heating phase. During the liquid heating phase, the temperature of the substance increases from $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $110^{\circ}\text{C}$ in the time interval from $t = 7\text{ min}$ to $t = 8\text{ min}$. The specific heat capacity of the substance in its liquid phase is ________ $\text{J kg}^{-1}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$.
questions.question: A solid substance of mass $2\text{ kg}$ is heated uniformly by a constant power source of $500\text{ W}$. The temperature-time heating curve of the substance shows a solid heating phase, a melting plateau, and a liquid heating phase. During the liquid heating phase, the temperature of the substance increases from $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $110^{\circ}\text{C}$ in the time interval from $t = 7\text{ min}$ to $t = 8\text{ min}$. The specific heat capacity of the substance in its liquid phase is ________ $\text{J kg}^{-1}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$.
questions.solution:
The time taken for the liquid phase to heat up is:
$\Delta t = 8\text{ min} - 7\text{ min} = 1\text{ min} = 60\text{ s}$

Total heat supplied during this phase:
$Q = P \times \Delta t = 500 \times 60 = 30000\text{ J}$

The change in temperature is:
$\Delta T = 110^{\circ}\text{C} - 80^{\circ}\text{C} = 30^{\circ}\text{C}$

Using the sensible heat formula $Q = mc\Delta T$:
$30000 = 2 \times c \times 30$
$30000 = 60c$

$c = \dfrac{30000}{60} = 500\text{ J kg}^{-1}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$

Answer: $500$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A faulty thermometer records a reading of $4^{\circ}\text{C}$ in melting ice. When the true temperature of a bath is $60^{\circ}\text{C}$, this thermometer reads $58^{\circ}\text{C}$. The reading of the faulty thermometer in boiling water is ______ $^{\circ}\text{C}$.
questions.question: A faulty thermometer records a reading of $4^{\circ}\text{C}$ in melting ice. When the true temperature of a bath is $60^{\circ}\text{C}$, this thermometer reads $58^{\circ}\text{C}$. The reading of the faulty thermometer in boiling water is ______ $^{\circ}\text{C}$.
questions.solution:
Let the reading of the faulty thermometer in boiling water (Upper Fixed Point) be $U$.

Using the principle of linear interpolation for temperature scales, we have:
$\dfrac{T_{\text{faulty}} - \text{LFP}}{U - \text{LFP}} = \dfrac{T_{\text{true}} - 0}{100 - 0}$

Substitute the given values:
$\dfrac{58 - 4}{U - 4} = \dfrac{60}{100}$

$\dfrac{54}{U - 4} = \dfrac{3}{5}$

$U - 4 = 54 \times \dfrac{5}{3}$

$U - 4 = 90$

$U = 94^{\circ}\text{C}$

Answer: $94$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal rod has a length of $100.00\text{ cm}$ at the freezing point of water. A new temperature scale $W$ is defined on which the freezing point of water is $20^{\circ}\text{W}$ and the boiling point of water is $170^{\circ}\text{W}$. When the rod is heated to a temperature of $95^{\circ}\text{W}$, its new length is found to be $100.10\text{ cm}$. The coefficient of linear expansion of the metal in $^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$ is:
questions.question: A metal rod has a length of $100.00\text{ cm}$ at the freezing point of water. A new temperature scale $W$ is defined on which the freezing point of water is $20^{\circ}\text{W}$ and the boiling point of water is $170^{\circ}\text{W}$. When the rod is heated to a temperature of $95^{\circ}\text{W}$, its new length is found to be $100.10\text{ cm}$. The coefficient of linear expansion of the metal in $^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$ is:
questions.solution:
First, we find the temperature of the rod on the Celsius scale when it is at $95^{\circ}\text{W}$. The relationship between scale $W$ and the Celsius scale is:

$\dfrac{t_W - 20}{170 - 20} = \dfrac{t_C - 0}{100 - 0}$

$\dfrac{95 - 20}{150} = \dfrac{t_C}{100}$

$\dfrac{75}{150} = \dfrac{t_C}{100}$

$t_C = 50^{\circ}\text{C}$

The initial temperature of the rod is the freezing point of water, which is $0^{\circ}\text{C}$. Therefore, the change in temperature is:

$\Delta t_C = 50^{\circ}\text{C} - 0^{\circ}\text{C} = 50^{\circ}\text{C}$

The change in length of the rod is:

$\Delta L = 100.10\text{ cm} - 100.00\text{ cm} = 0.10\text{ cm}$

Using the formula for linear expansion, $\Delta L = L_0 \alpha \Delta t_C$:

$0.10 = 100.00 \times \alpha \times 50$

$0.10 = 5000 \alpha$

$\alpha = \dfrac{0.10}{5000} = 2.0 \times 10^{-5} \, ^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$

Answer: $2.0 \times 10^{-5} \, ^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A composite rod is formed by joining two different materials A and B in series. Rod A has a length of $16\text{ cm}$ and thermal conductivity $200\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. Rod B has a length of $12\text{ cm}$ and thermal conductivity $100\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. Both rods have the same uniform cross-sectional area of $4\text{ cm}^2$. The free end of rod A is kept in a steam bath at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ while the free end of rod B is kept in an ice bath at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$. Assuming no heat loss from the curved surfaces, the mass of ice (in grams) that melts in $168\text{ s}$ is ________.

[Given: Latent heat of fusion of ice $= 336\text{ J g}^{-1}$]
questions.question:
A composite rod is formed by joining two different materials A and B in series. Rod A has a length of $16\text{ cm}$ and thermal conductivity $200\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. Rod B has a length of $12\text{ cm}$ and thermal conductivity $100\text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$. Both rods have the same uniform cross-sectional area of $4\text{ cm}^2$. The free end of rod A is kept in a steam bath at $100^{\circ}\text{C}$ while the free end of rod B is kept in an ice bath at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$. Assuming no heat loss from the curved surfaces, the mass of ice (in grams) that melts in $168\text{ s}$ is ________.

[Given: Latent heat of fusion of ice $= 336\text{ J g}^{-1}$]
questions.solution:
The thermal resistance of a rod is given by $R = \dfrac{L}{KA}$.

For rod A:
$L_A = 16 \text{ cm} = 0.16 \text{ m}$
$K_A = 200 \text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$
$A = 4 \text{ cm}^2 = 4 \times 10^{-4} \text{ m}^2$
$R_A = \dfrac{0.16}{200 \times 4 \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{0.16}{0.08} = 2 \text{ K W}^{-1}$

For rod B:
$L_B = 12 \text{ cm} = 0.12 \text{ m}$
$K_B = 100 \text{ W m}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$
$R_B = \dfrac{0.12}{100 \times 4 \times 10^{-4}} = \dfrac{0.12}{0.04} = 3 \text{ K W}^{-1}$

Since the rods are in series, the equivalent thermal resistance is:
$R_{eq} = R_A + R_B = 2 + 3 = 5 \text{ K W}^{-1}$

The steady heat current $H$ is:
$H = \dfrac{\Delta T}{R_{eq}} = \dfrac{100 - 0}{5} = 20 \text{ W}$

The total heat transferred in $t = 168 \text{ s}$ is:
$Q = H \times t = 20 \times 168 = 3360 \text{ J}$

Let $m$ be the mass of ice melted. Using $Q = m L_f$:
$3360 = m \times 336$

$m = 10 \text{ g}$

Answer: $10$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A new temperature scale $X$ is defined such that the freezing point of water is $-20^{\circ}\text{X}$ and the boiling point of water is $130^{\circ}\text{X}$. At what temperature on the Celsius scale will the reading on scale $X$ be exactly double the reading on the Celsius scale?
questions.question: A new temperature scale $X$ is defined such that the freezing point of water is $-20^{\circ}\text{X}$ and the boiling point of water is $130^{\circ}\text{X}$. At what temperature on the Celsius scale will the reading on scale $X$ be exactly double the reading on the Celsius scale?
questions.solution:
The relationship between the new scale $X$ and the Celsius scale is given by equating the ratio of temperature differences:

$\dfrac{t_X - \text{LFP}_X}{\text{UFP}_X - \text{LFP}_X} = \dfrac{t_C - \text{LFP}_C}{\text{UFP}_C - \text{LFP}_C}$

Substituting the given fixed points for scale $X$ ($-20^{\circ}\text{X}$ and $130^{\circ}\text{X}$) and the Celsius scale ($0^{\circ}\text{C}$ and $100^{\circ}\text{C}$):

$\dfrac{t_X - (-20)}{130 - (-20)} = \dfrac{t_C - 0}{100 - 0}$

$\dfrac{t_X + 20}{150} = \dfrac{t_C}{100}$

$\dfrac{t_X + 20}{3} = \dfrac{t_C}{2}$

We are given the condition that the reading on scale $X$ is twice the reading on the Celsius scale, so $t_X = 2t_C$. Substituting this into the equation:

$\dfrac{2t_C + 20}{3} = \dfrac{t_C}{2}$

Cross-multiplying yields:

$2(2t_C + 20) = 3t_C$

$4t_C + 40 = 3t_C$

$t_C = -40^{\circ}\text{C}$

Answer: $-40^{\circ}\text{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A liquid having a heat capacity of $1800 \text{ J K}^{-1}$ cools from $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $12$ minutes. The temperature of the surroundings is $20^{\circ}\text{C}$. An electrical heater is now immersed in the liquid to maintain its temperature at a steady $80^{\circ}\text{C}$. Assuming Newton's law of cooling is valid, the power of the heater required is ________ $\text{W}$.
questions.question: A liquid having a heat capacity of $1800 \text{ J K}^{-1}$ cools from $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $12$ minutes. The temperature of the surroundings is $20^{\circ}\text{C}$. An electrical heater is now immersed in the liquid to maintain its temperature at a steady $80^{\circ}\text{C}$. Assuming Newton's law of cooling is valid, the power of the heater required is ________ $\text{W}$.
questions.solution:
Using the average temperature approximation of Newton's law of cooling for the first process:
$\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta t} = K\left(\dfrac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0\right)$

The liquid cools from $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $60^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $12$ minutes:
$\dfrac{80 - 60}{12} = K\left(\dfrac{80 + 60}{2} - 20\right)$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{20}{12} = K(70 - 20)$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{5}{3} = K(50)$
$\Rightarrow K = \dfrac{1}{30} \text{ min}^{-1}$

To maintain the liquid at a steady temperature of $80^{\circ}\text{C}$, the heater must supply heat at the same rate the liquid loses heat to the surroundings at $80^{\circ}\text{C}$.
The rate of cooling at $80^{\circ}\text{C}$ is:
$\dfrac{dT}{dt} = K(T - T_0) = \dfrac{1}{30}(80 - 20) = \dfrac{60}{30} = 2^{\circ}\text{C min}^{-1}$

The rate of heat loss is:
$\dfrac{dQ}{dt} = C \dfrac{dT}{dt} = 1800 \times 2 = 3600 \text{ J min}^{-1}$

Converting this to Watts (Joules per second):
$P = \dfrac{3600 \text{ J}}{60 \text{ s}} = 60 \text{ W}$

Answer: $60$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
An aluminium block of mass $840 \text{ g}$ at a temperature of $200^\circ\text{C}$ is placed in a cavity within a large block of ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$. The mass of ice that melts before the aluminium block cools down to $0^\circ\text{C}$ is $x \text{ g}$. The value of $x$ is ________.

[Use: Specific heat capacity of aluminium $= 900 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, Latent heat of fusion of ice $= 3.36 \times 10^5 \text{ J kg}^{-1}$]
questions.question:
An aluminium block of mass $840 \text{ g}$ at a temperature of $200^\circ\text{C}$ is placed in a cavity within a large block of ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$. The mass of ice that melts before the aluminium block cools down to $0^\circ\text{C}$ is $x \text{ g}$. The value of $x$ is ________.

[Use: Specific heat capacity of aluminium $= 900 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{K}^{-1}$, Latent heat of fusion of ice $= 3.36 \times 10^5 \text{ J kg}^{-1}$]
questions.solution:
The final temperature of the aluminium block will be $0^\circ\text{C}$ since it is placed in a large block of ice.

Heat lost by the aluminium block as it cools from $200^\circ\text{C}$ to $0^\circ\text{C}$:
$\Delta Q = m_{\text{Al}} s_{\text{Al}} \Delta T$
$\Delta Q = 0.84 \times 900 \times 200$
$\Delta Q = 151200 \text{ J}$

This heat is entirely used to melt $x \text{ g}$ of ice at $0^\circ\text{C}$.
Heat gained by the ice:
$\Delta Q = m_{\text{ice}} L$
$151200 = m_{\text{ice}} \times 3.36 \times 10^5$

Solving for $m_{\text{ice}}$:
$m_{\text{ice}} = \dfrac{151200}{336000} = 0.45 \text{ kg}$

Converting to grams:
$x = 0.45 \times 1000 = 450 \text{ g}$

Answer: $450$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A cooling system uses ice at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ to absorb heat rejected by a machine operating at a constant power of $4.2\text{ kW}$. The ice completely melts and leaves the system as water at $20^{\circ}\text{C}$. The mass of ice consumed per second by the cooling system is ________ $\text{g}$.

(Given: Latent heat of fusion of ice = $336 \times 10^3\text{ J kg}^{-1}$, Specific heat capacity of water = $4200\text{ J kg}^{-1}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$)
questions.question:
A cooling system uses ice at $0^{\circ}\text{C}$ to absorb heat rejected by a machine operating at a constant power of $4.2\text{ kW}$. The ice completely melts and leaves the system as water at $20^{\circ}\text{C}$. The mass of ice consumed per second by the cooling system is ________ $\text{g}$.

(Given: Latent heat of fusion of ice = $336 \times 10^3\text{ J kg}^{-1}$, Specific heat capacity of water = $4200\text{ J kg}^{-1}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
Let the mass of ice consumed per second be $m$ (in kg).

The heat absorbed per second by the ice is the sum of the heat required to melt the ice and the heat required to raise the temperature of the resulting water to $20^{\circ}\text{C}$.

Rate of heat absorption, $P = m(L_f + c_w \Delta T)$

Given:
$P = 4.2\text{ kW} = 4200\text{ J s}^{-1}$
$L_f = 336000\text{ J kg}^{-1}$
$c_w = 4200\text{ J kg}^{-1}^{\circ}\text{C}^{-1}$
$\Delta T = 20 - 0 = 20^{\circ}\text{C}$

Substituting the values:
$4200 = m(336000 + 4200 \times 20)$
$4200 = m(336000 + 84000)$
$4200 = m(420000)$

$m = \dfrac{4200}{420000} = 0.01\text{ kg s}^{-1}$

Converting to grams:
$m = 0.01 \times 1000\text{ g s}^{-1} = 10\text{ g s}^{-1}$

Answer: $10$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A hot body cools from $90^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $70^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $4$ minutes. In the next $6$ minutes, its temperature drops from $70^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $50^{\circ}\text{C}$. Assuming Newton's law of cooling holds true, the temperature of the surroundings is ________ $^{\circ}\text{C}$.
questions.question: A hot body cools from $90^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $70^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $4$ minutes. In the next $6$ minutes, its temperature drops from $70^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $50^{\circ}\text{C}$. Assuming Newton's law of cooling holds true, the temperature of the surroundings is ________ $^{\circ}\text{C}$.
questions.solution:
According to the average temperature approximation of Newton's law of cooling:
$\dfrac{\Delta T}{\Delta t} = K\left(\dfrac{T_1 + T_2}{2} - T_0\right)$

For the first interval (cooling from $90^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $70^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $4$ minutes):
$\dfrac{90 - 70}{4} = K\left(\dfrac{90 + 70}{2} - T_0\right)$
$\Rightarrow 5 = K(80 - T_0)$ ... (i)

For the second interval (cooling from $70^{\circ}\text{C}$ to $50^{\circ}\text{C}$ in $6$ minutes):
$\dfrac{70 - 50}{6} = K\left(\dfrac{70 + 50}{2} - T_0\right)$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{10}{3} = K(60 - T_0)$ ... (ii)

Dividing equation (i) by equation (ii):
$\dfrac{5}{\left(\dfrac{10}{3}\right)} = \dfrac{80 - T_0}{60 - T_0}$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{15}{10} = \dfrac{80 - T_0}{60 - T_0}$
$\Rightarrow 1.5 = \dfrac{80 - T_0}{60 - T_0}$

Cross-multiplying yields:
$1.5(60 - T_0) = 80 - T_0$
$90 - 1.5T_0 = 80 - T_0$
$10 = 0.5T_0$
$\Rightarrow T_0 = 20^{\circ}\text{C}$

Answer: $20$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A rigid cylinder of volume $67.2\ \text{L}$ initially contains a mixture of helium and nitrogen gases at standard temperature and pressure. The total mass of the gas mixture is $36\ \text{g}$. The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of the gas mixture in the cylinder by $10.0^\circ\text{C}$ is (Given gas constant $R=8.3\ \text{J}\ \text{K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)
questions.question: A rigid cylinder of volume $67.2\ \text{L}$ initially contains a mixture of helium and nitrogen gases at standard temperature and pressure. The total mass of the gas mixture is $36\ \text{g}$. The amount of heat required to raise the temperature of the gas mixture in the cylinder by $10.0^\circ\text{C}$ is (Given gas constant $R=8.3\ \text{J}\ \text{K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$)
questions.solution:
At STP, the volume occupied by one mole of an ideal gas is $22.4\ \text{L}$.
The total number of moles in the mixture is:
$n_{\text{total}} = \dfrac{67.2}{22.4} = 3\ \text{mol}$

Let $n_{\text{He}}$ and $n_{\text{N}_2}$ be the number of moles of helium and nitrogen, respectively.
$n_{\text{He}} + n_{\text{N}_2} = 3$

The total mass of the mixture is $36\ \text{g}$. The molar mass of He is $4\ \text{g/mol}$ and of $N_2$ is $28\ \text{g/mol}$.
$4n_{\text{He}} + 28n_{\text{N}_2} = 36$

Substituting $n_{\text{N}_2} = 3 - n_{\text{He}}$ into the mass equation:
$4n_{\text{He}} + 28(3 - n_{\text{He}}) = 36$
$4n_{\text{He}} + 84 - 28n_{\text{He}} = 36$
$24n_{\text{He}} = 48 \Rightarrow n_{\text{He}} = 2\ \text{mol}$
Thus, $n_{\text{N}_2} = 1\ \text{mol}$.

The process is isochoric (rigid cylinder). The molar heat capacities at constant volume are:
$C_{v,\text{He}} = \dfrac{3}{2}R$ (monoatomic)
$C_{v,\text{N}_2} = \dfrac{5}{2}R$ (diatomic)

The total heat required is:
$Q = (n_{\text{He}} C_{v,\text{He}} + n_{\text{N}_2} C_{v,\text{N}_2}) \Delta T$
$Q = \left(2 \times \dfrac{3}{2}R + 1 \times \dfrac{5}{2}R\right) \times 10$
$Q = (3R + 2.5R) \times 10 = 5.5R \times 10 = 55R$

Substituting $R = 8.3\ \text{J}\ \text{K}^{-1}\ \text{mol}^{-1}$:
$Q = 55 \times 8.3 = 456.5\ \text{J}$

Answer: $456.5\ \text{J}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A block slides down a rough inclined plane of length $250$ m at a constant speed. The angle of inclination of the plane is $37^\circ$ with the horizontal. If $50\%$ of the heat generated due to friction is absorbed by the block, what will be the rise in the temperature of the block?

[Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$, specific heat capacity of the block $s = 500$ J/(kg $^\circ$C) and $\sin(37^\circ) = 0.6$]
questions.question:
A block slides down a rough inclined plane of length $250$ m at a constant speed. The angle of inclination of the plane is $37^\circ$ with the horizontal. If $50\%$ of the heat generated due to friction is absorbed by the block, what will be the rise in the temperature of the block?

[Take $g = 10$ m/s$^2$, specific heat capacity of the block $s = 500$ J/(kg $^\circ$C) and $\sin(37^\circ) = 0.6$]
questions.solution:
Since the block moves at a constant speed, its kinetic energy does not change. The work done against friction is equal to the loss in gravitational potential energy.

Loss in potential energy $= mgh = mgL\sin(37^\circ)$
$= m \times 10 \times 250 \times 0.6 = 1500m$ J

Heat generated by friction $= 1500m$ J
Heat absorbed by the block, $Q = 50\%$ of $1500m = 750m$ J

Using the calorimetry principle $Q = ms\Delta T$:
$750m = m \times 500 \times \Delta T$
$\Delta T = \dfrac{750}{500} = 1.5^\circ$C

Answer: $1.5^\circ$C

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Three distinct metal rods of identical length and uniform cross-sectional area are joined together at a common central junction to form a Y-shape. The free ends of the rods are maintained at steady temperatures of $90^\circ\text{C}$, $60^\circ\text{C}$, and $0^\circ\text{C}$. The thermal conductivities of the rods connected to these ends are $K$, $2K$, and $3K$, respectively. Assuming no heat loss to the surroundings, the steady-state temperature of the central junction is:
questions.question: Three distinct metal rods of identical length and uniform cross-sectional area are joined together at a common central junction to form a Y-shape. The free ends of the rods are maintained at steady temperatures of $90^\circ\text{C}$, $60^\circ\text{C}$, and $0^\circ\text{C}$. The thermal conductivities of the rods connected to these ends are $K$, $2K$, and $3K$, respectively. Assuming no heat loss to the surroundings, the steady-state temperature of the central junction is:
questions.solution:
Let the steady-state temperature of the central junction be $T$.

According to the principle of conservation of energy, the net heat current into the junction must be zero in steady state.

$\sum H = 0$

$\dfrac{K A (90 - T)}{L} + \dfrac{2K A (60 - T)}{L} + \dfrac{3K A (0 - T)}{L} = 0$

Cancelling the common terms $\dfrac{K A}{L}$:
$(90 - T) + 2(60 - T) + 3(0 - T) = 0$

$\Rightarrow 90 - T + 120 - 2T - 3T = 0$

$\Rightarrow 210 - 6T = 0$

$\Rightarrow 6T = 210$

$\Rightarrow T = 35^\circ\text{C}$

Answer: $35^\circ\text{C}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A block of ice at $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ falls from a height $h$ and hits the ground perfectly inelastically. Assuming that all of the lost mechanical energy is absorbed by the ice, find the height $h$ from which the ice must fall so that exactly one-quarter of its mass melts.
(Take $g = 10 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$ and latent heat of fusion of ice $L = 3.36 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~J/kg}$)
questions.question:
A block of ice at $0^{\circ}\mathrm{C}$ falls from a height $h$ and hits the ground perfectly inelastically. Assuming that all of the lost mechanical energy is absorbed by the ice, find the height $h$ from which the ice must fall so that exactly one-quarter of its mass melts.
(Take $g = 10 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$ and latent heat of fusion of ice $L = 3.36 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~J/kg}$)
questions.solution:
Let the total mass of the ice block be $m$.

The gravitational potential energy lost by the ice block when it falls from height $h$ is:
$U = mgh$

The heat energy required to melt one-quarter of the mass of the ice is:
$Q = \left(\dfrac{m}{4}\right)L$

Since all the lost mechanical energy is absorbed by the ice as heat, we equate $U$ and $Q$:
$mgh = \dfrac{mL}{4}$

The total mass $m$ cancels out from both sides:
$gh = \dfrac{L}{4}$

Rearranging for $h$:
$h = \dfrac{L}{4g}$

Substitute the given values ($L = 3.36 \times 10^5 \mathrm{~J/kg}$ and $g = 10 \mathrm{~m/s^2}$):
$h = \dfrac{3.36 \times 10^5}{4 \times 10}$
$h = \dfrac{336000}{40}$
$h = 8400 \mathrm{~m}$

Answer: $8400 \mathrm{~m}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal sphere moving at a high speed $v$ strikes a rigid target and comes to a complete halt. It is found that $80\%$ of its lost kinetic energy is absorbed by the sphere itself as heat. This absorbed heat is just enough to raise its temperature from $300 \text{ K}$ to its melting point of $700 \text{ K}$ and melt it completely. If the specific heat capacity of the metal is $250 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ and its latent heat of fusion is $4.4 \times 10^4 \text{ J kg}^{-1}$, the initial speed $v$ of the sphere is:
questions.question: A metal sphere moving at a high speed $v$ strikes a rigid target and comes to a complete halt. It is found that $80\%$ of its lost kinetic energy is absorbed by the sphere itself as heat. This absorbed heat is just enough to raise its temperature from $300 \text{ K}$ to its melting point of $700 \text{ K}$ and melt it completely. If the specific heat capacity of the metal is $250 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$ and its latent heat of fusion is $4.4 \times 10^4 \text{ J kg}^{-1}$, the initial speed $v$ of the sphere is:
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the sphere be $m$. The initial kinetic energy of the sphere is $K = \dfrac{1}{2} m v^2$.

The heat absorbed by the sphere is $80\%$ of its initial kinetic energy:
$Q = 0.8 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2} m v^2\right) = 0.4 m v^2$

This heat is utilized in two stages: raising the temperature to the melting point (sensible heat) and melting the sphere completely (latent heat).
$Q = m c \Delta T + mL$

Equating the two expressions for $Q$:
$0.4 m v^2 = m (c \Delta T + L)$

The mass $m$ cancels out from both sides:
$0.4 v^2 = c (T_2 - T_1) + L$

Substitute the given values ($c = 250 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$, $T_1 = 300 \text{ K}$, $T_2 = 700 \text{ K}$, $L = 4.4 \times 10^4 \text{ J kg}^{-1}$):
$0.4 v^2 = 250 \times (700 - 300) + 4.4 \times 10^4$
$0.4 v^2 = 250 \times 400 + 44000$
$0.4 v^2 = 100000 + 44000$
$0.4 v^2 = 144000$

Solving for $v^2$:
$v^2 = \dfrac{144000}{0.4} = 360000$

Taking the square root:
$v = 600 \text{ m/s}$

Answer: $600 \text{ m/s}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A composite rod of uniform cross-section is made of two different materials A and B connected in series. The steady-state temperature distribution along the length of the rod is plotted as a graph of temperature ($T$) versus distance ($x$) from the hotter end. The graph consists of two straight line segments: the first segment for material A goes from $(x=0\text{ cm}, T=100^\circ\text{C})$ to $(x=10\text{ cm}, T=60^\circ\text{C})$, and the second segment for material B goes from $(x=10\text{ cm}, T=60^\circ\text{C})$ to $(x=30\text{ cm}, T=0^\circ\text{C})$. The ratio of the thermal conductivities of the two materials, $\dfrac{K_A}{K_B}$, is:
questions.question: A composite rod of uniform cross-section is made of two different materials A and B connected in series. The steady-state temperature distribution along the length of the rod is plotted as a graph of temperature ($T$) versus distance ($x$) from the hotter end. The graph consists of two straight line segments: the first segment for material A goes from $(x=0\text{ cm}, T=100^\circ\text{C})$ to $(x=10\text{ cm}, T=60^\circ\text{C})$, and the second segment for material B goes from $(x=10\text{ cm}, T=60^\circ\text{C})$ to $(x=30\text{ cm}, T=0^\circ\text{C})$. The ratio of the thermal conductivities of the two materials, $\dfrac{K_A}{K_B}$, is:
questions.solution:
In steady state, the heat current $H$ is the same through both materials.

The magnitude of the temperature gradient for material A is:
$\left|\dfrac{dT}{dx}\right|_A = \dfrac{100 - 60}{10 - 0} = 4^\circ\text{C/cm}$

The magnitude of the temperature gradient for material B is:
$\left|\dfrac{dT}{dx}\right|_B = \dfrac{60 - 0}{30 - 10} = \dfrac{60}{20} = 3^\circ\text{C/cm}$

Using Fourier's law of heat conduction, $H = K A \left|\dfrac{dT}{dx}\right|$.

Equating the heat currents for the two materials in series:
$K_A A (4) = K_B A (3)$

$\Rightarrow \dfrac{K_A}{K_B} = \dfrac{3}{4}$

Answer: $\dfrac{3}{4}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A metal shaft has a diameter of $5.015 \text{ cm}$ at $50^\circ\text{C}$. A bearing has an inner diameter of $5.000 \text{ cm}$ at the same temperature. The bearing is heated so that the shaft exactly slides into it. If the bearing must be heated to $250^\circ\text{C}$ for this exact fit, what is the coefficient of linear expansion of the bearing material? (Assume the shaft remains at $50^\circ\text{C}$ during the process)
questions.question: A metal shaft has a diameter of $5.015 \text{ cm}$ at $50^\circ\text{C}$. A bearing has an inner diameter of $5.000 \text{ cm}$ at the same temperature. The bearing is heated so that the shaft exactly slides into it. If the bearing must be heated to $250^\circ\text{C}$ for this exact fit, what is the coefficient of linear expansion of the bearing material? (Assume the shaft remains at $50^\circ\text{C}$ during the process)
questions.solution:
The initial inner diameter of the bearing is $D_0 = 5.000 \text{ cm}$ at $T_1 = 50^\circ\text{C}$.

For the shaft to exactly slide in, the final inner diameter of the bearing must be equal to the diameter of the shaft, so $D = 5.015 \text{ cm}$.

The required expansion in the diameter is:
$\Delta D = D - D_0 = 5.015 - 5.000 = 0.015 \text{ cm}$

The change in temperature of the bearing is:
$\Delta T = T_2 - T_1 = 250^\circ\text{C} - 50^\circ\text{C} = 200^\circ\text{C}$

Using the formula for linear expansion, $\Delta D = D_0 \alpha \Delta T$, we can solve for the coefficient of linear expansion $\alpha$:
$\alpha = \dfrac{\Delta D}{D_0 \Delta T}$

$\alpha = \dfrac{0.015}{5.000 \times 200}$

$\alpha = \dfrac{0.015}{1000} = 1.5 \times 10^{-5} ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$

Answer: $1.5 \times 10^{-5} ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A faulty thermometer reads $2^{\circ}\text{C}$ in melting ice and $92^{\circ}\text{C}$ in boiling water. The true temperature on the Celsius scale at which this faulty thermometer gives the exact same numerical reading is ______ $^{\circ}\text{C}$.
questions.question: A faulty thermometer reads $2^{\circ}\text{C}$ in melting ice and $92^{\circ}\text{C}$ in boiling water. The true temperature on the Celsius scale at which this faulty thermometer gives the exact same numerical reading is ______ $^{\circ}\text{C}$.
questions.solution:
Let the temperature at which both the faulty thermometer and the correct Celsius thermometer show the same numerical reading be $T$.

Using the relation between the two scales:
$\dfrac{T_{\text{faulty}} - \text{LFP}}{\text{UFP} - \text{LFP}} = \dfrac{T_{\text{true}} - 0}{100 - 0}$

Substitute the known values and set $T_{\text{faulty}} = T_{\text{true}} = T$:
$\dfrac{T - 2}{92 - 2} = \dfrac{T}{100}$

$\dfrac{T - 2}{90} = \dfrac{T}{100}$

Cross-multiplying gives:
$10(T - 2) = 9T$

$10T - 20 = 9T$

$T = 20^{\circ}\text{C}$

Answer: $20$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid metallic cube of side length $10 \text{ cm}$ and mass $2 \text{ kg}$ is heated by supplying $8000 \text{ J}$ of thermal energy. The specific heat capacity of the metal is $400 \text{ J kg}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1}$ and its coefficient of linear expansion is $2.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ K}^{-1}$. The change in the volume of the cube is :
questions.question: A solid metallic cube of side length $10 \text{ cm}$ and mass $2 \text{ kg}$ is heated by supplying $8000 \text{ J}$ of thermal energy. The specific heat capacity of the metal is $400 \text{ J kg}^{-1} \text{ K}^{-1}$ and its coefficient of linear expansion is $2.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ K}^{-1}$. The change in the volume of the cube is :
questions.solution:
The heat supplied to the cube is given by:
$\Delta Q = m c \Delta T$

Substituting the given values to find the rise in temperature:
$8000 = 2 \times 400 \times \Delta T$
$\Delta T = \dfrac{8000}{800} = 10 \text{ K}$

The initial volume of the cube is:
$V_0 = (10 \text{ cm})^3 = (0.1 \text{ m})^3 = 10^{-3} \text{ m}^3$

The coefficient of volume expansion is $\gamma = 3\alpha$.
The change in volume is:
$\Delta V = V_0 \gamma \Delta T = V_0 (3\alpha) \Delta T$
$\Delta V = 10^{-3} \times (3 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-5}) \times 10$
$\Delta V = 10^{-3} \times 6.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 10 = 6.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^3$

Answer: $6.0 \times 10^{-7} \text{ m}^3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid sample is heated by an electrical heater of constant power. The temperature-time graph of the process shows that the temperature of the solid rises linearly from $300 \text{ K}$ to its melting point of $500 \text{ K}$ in $2 \text{ minutes}$. It then remains constant at $500 \text{ K}$ for the next $5 \text{ minutes}$ until the sample melts completely. If the specific heat capacity of the solid is $400 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$, the latent heat of fusion of the material is:
questions.question: A solid sample is heated by an electrical heater of constant power. The temperature-time graph of the process shows that the temperature of the solid rises linearly from $300 \text{ K}$ to its melting point of $500 \text{ K}$ in $2 \text{ minutes}$. It then remains constant at $500 \text{ K}$ for the next $5 \text{ minutes}$ until the sample melts completely. If the specific heat capacity of the solid is $400 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$, the latent heat of fusion of the material is:
questions.solution:
Let the constant power of the heater be $P$ and the mass of the sample be $m$.

During the first $2 \text{ minutes}$ ($t_1$), the heat supplied raises the temperature of the solid:
$P t_1 = m c \Delta T$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{P}{m} = \dfrac{c (T_{\text{melt}} - T_{\text{initial}})}{t_1}$

During the next $5 \text{ minutes}$ ($t_2$), the heat supplied melts the solid at constant temperature:
$P t_2 = mL$
$\Rightarrow \dfrac{P}{m} = \dfrac{L}{t_2}$

Equating the two expressions for $\dfrac{P}{m}$:
$\dfrac{L}{t_2} = \dfrac{c (T_{\text{melt}} - T_{\text{initial}})}{t_1}$

Rearranging for the latent heat of fusion $L$:
$L = c (T_{\text{melt}} - T_{\text{initial}}) \times \dfrac{t_2}{t_1}$

Substitute the given values ($c = 400 \text{ J kg}^{-1}\text{ K}^{-1}$, $T_{\text{melt}} = 500 \text{ K}$, $T_{\text{initial}} = 300 \text{ K}$, $t_1 = 2 \text{ min}$, $t_2 = 5 \text{ min}$):
$L = 400 \times (500 - 300) \times \dfrac{5}{2}$
$L = 400 \times 200 \times 2.5$
$L = 80000 \times 2.5 = 200000 \text{ J kg}^{-1} = 2.0 \times 10^5 \text{ J kg}^{-1}$

Answer: $2.0 \times 10^5 \text{ J kg}^{-1}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A metallic rod of length $2$ m is moving longitudinally on a smooth horizontal surface with a velocity of $200$ m/s. It undergoes a perfectly inelastic collision with a rigid wall and comes to rest. If $40\%$ of its initial kinetic energy is converted into heat and absorbed entirely by the rod, what will be the increase in the length of the rod?

[Given: Specific heat capacity of the rod $s = 500$ J/(kg $^\circ$C) and coefficient of linear expansion $\alpha = 1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ /$^\circ$C]
questions.question:
A metallic rod of length $2$ m is moving longitudinally on a smooth horizontal surface with a velocity of $200$ m/s. It undergoes a perfectly inelastic collision with a rigid wall and comes to rest. If $40\%$ of its initial kinetic energy is converted into heat and absorbed entirely by the rod, what will be the increase in the length of the rod?

[Given: Specific heat capacity of the rod $s = 500$ J/(kg $^\circ$C) and coefficient of linear expansion $\alpha = 1.5 \times 10^{-5}$ /$^\circ$C]
questions.solution:
Initial kinetic energy of the rod is given by:
$KE = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2 = \dfrac{1}{2}m(200)^2 = 20000m$ J

Heat absorbed by the rod is $40\%$ of the initial kinetic energy:
$Q = 0.40 \times 20000m = 8000m$ J

Using the calorimetry principle $Q = ms\Delta T$:
$8000m = m \times 500 \times \Delta T$
$\Delta T = \dfrac{8000}{500} = 16^\circ$C

The increase in the length of the rod is:
$\Delta L = L\alpha\Delta T$
$\Delta L = 2 \times 1.5 \times 10^{-5} \times 16 = 48 \times 10^{-5}$ m

Converting to millimeters:
$\Delta L = 48 \times 10^{-5} \times 10^3$ mm $= 0.48$ mm

Answer: $0.48$ mm

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid metallic sphere has an initial volume of $36\pi \text{ m}^3$. It is heated uniformly such that its temperature increases by $50^\circ\text{C}$. If the coefficient of volume expansion of the metal is $6.0 \times 10^{-5} \, ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$, the increase in the surface area of the sphere is:
questions.question: A solid metallic sphere has an initial volume of $36\pi \text{ m}^3$. It is heated uniformly such that its temperature increases by $50^\circ\text{C}$. If the coefficient of volume expansion of the metal is $6.0 \times 10^{-5} \, ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$, the increase in the surface area of the sphere is:
questions.solution:
Let the initial radius of the sphere be $R$.

The initial volume of the sphere is given by:
$V_0 = \dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3$

Given $V_0 = 36\pi \text{ m}^3$, we have:
$\dfrac{4}{3}\pi R^3 = 36\pi \Rightarrow R^3 = 27 \Rightarrow R = 3 \text{ m}$

The initial surface area of the sphere is:
$A_0 = 4\pi R^2 = 4\pi (3)^2 = 36\pi \text{ m}^2$

The coefficient of areal expansion $\beta$ is related to the coefficient of volume expansion $\gamma$ by:
$\beta = \dfrac{2}{3}\gamma = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 6.0 \times 10^{-5} = 4.0 \times 10^{-5} \, ^\circ\text{C}^{-1}$

The increase in surface area $\Delta A$ is:
$\Delta A = A_0 \beta \Delta T$
$\Delta A = (36\pi) \times (4.0 \times 10^{-5}) \times 50$
$\Delta A = 36\pi \times 200 \times 10^{-5} = 0.072\pi \text{ m}^2$

Converting to $\text{cm}^2$ ($1 \text{ m}^2 = 10^4 \text{ cm}^2$):
$\Delta A = 0.072\pi \times 10^4 \text{ cm}^2 = 720\pi \text{ cm}^2$

Answer: $720\pi \text{ cm}^2$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q:
A lead bullet moving with a speed of $400 \mathrm{~m/s}$ strikes a rigid wall and comes to a complete halt. Assuming that $50\%$ of the kinetic energy lost is absorbed by the bullet as heat, calculate the rise in temperature of the bullet.
(Given: specific heat capacity of lead $= 125 \mathrm{~J/(kg \cdot K)}$)
questions.question:
A lead bullet moving with a speed of $400 \mathrm{~m/s}$ strikes a rigid wall and comes to a complete halt. Assuming that $50\%$ of the kinetic energy lost is absorbed by the bullet as heat, calculate the rise in temperature of the bullet.
(Given: specific heat capacity of lead $= 125 \mathrm{~J/(kg \cdot K)}$)
questions.solution:
Let the mass of the bullet be $m$.

The initial kinetic energy of the bullet is $K = \dfrac{1}{2}mv^2$.

The heat absorbed by the bullet is $50\%$ of this kinetic energy:
$Q = 0.5 \times \left(\dfrac{1}{2}mv^2\right) = 0.25 m v^2$

The heat absorbed is also given by $Q = ms\Delta T$, where $s$ is the specific heat capacity and $\Delta T$ is the rise in temperature.

Equating the two expressions for $Q$:
$0.25 m v^2 = ms\Delta T$

The mass $m$ cancels out:
$\Delta T = \dfrac{0.25 v^2}{s}$

Substitute the given values ($v = 400 \mathrm{~m/s}$ and $s = 125 \mathrm{~J/(kg \cdot K)}$):
$\Delta T = \dfrac{0.25 \times (400)^2}{125}$
$\Delta T = \dfrac{0.25 \times 160000}{125}$
$\Delta T = \dfrac{40000}{125} = 320 \mathrm{~K}$

Answer: $320 \mathrm{~K}$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: A solid metallic object is heated by supplying $4 \times 10^5 \text{ J}$ of heat energy. The density of the metal is $8000 \text{ kg/m}^3$, its specific heat capacity is $500 \text{ J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$, and its coefficient of linear expansion is $2.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ K}^{-1}$. The increase in the volume of the object is:
questions.question: A solid metallic object is heated by supplying $4 \times 10^5 \text{ J}$ of heat energy. The density of the metal is $8000 \text{ kg/m}^3$, its specific heat capacity is $500 \text{ J/(kg}\cdot\text{K)}$, and its coefficient of linear expansion is $2.0 \times 10^{-5} \text{ K}^{-1}$. The increase in the volume of the object is:
questions.solution:
The heat energy $Q$ supplied to the object is given by:
$Q = mc\Delta T$
where $m$ is the mass, $c$ is the specific heat capacity, and $\Delta T$ is the increase in temperature.

The mass of the object can be written in terms of its initial volume $V_0$ and density $\rho$ as $m = \rho V_0$.
Substituting this into the heat equation:
$Q = \rho V_0 c \Delta T \Rightarrow V_0 \Delta T = \dfrac{Q}{\rho c}$

The increase in volume $\Delta V$ is given by:
$\Delta V = V_0 \gamma \Delta T$
where $\gamma$ is the coefficient of volume expansion. For an isotropic solid, $\gamma = 3\alpha$.

Substituting $\gamma$ and $V_0 \Delta T$ into the equation for $\Delta V$:
$\Delta V = (3\alpha) \left( \dfrac{Q}{\rho c} \right)$

Now, substituting the given values:
$\Delta V = \dfrac{3 \times 2.0 \times 10^{-5} \times 4 \times 10^5}{8000 \times 500}$
$\Delta V = \dfrac{24}{4 \times 10^6} = 6.0 \times 10^{-6} \text{ m}^3$

Converting the volume increase to $\text{cm}^3$ ($1 \text{ m}^3 = 10^6 \text{ cm}^3$):
$\Delta V = 6.0 \times 10^{-6} \times 10^6 \text{ cm}^3 = 6 \text{ cm}^3$

Answer: $6 \text{ cm}^3$

questions.subject: Physics
questions.q: Two solid spheres, A and B, are made of different materials. The ratio of the density of A to that of B is $3 : 1$, the ratio of their specific heat capacities is $2 : 1$, and the ratio of their coefficients of linear expansion is $5 : 1$. If the same amount of heat is supplied to both spheres, the ratio of the change in volume of sphere A to the change in volume of sphere B is :
questions.question: Two solid spheres, A and B, are made of different materials. The ratio of the density of A to that of B is $3 : 1$, the ratio of their specific heat capacities is $2 : 1$, and the ratio of their coefficients of linear expansion is $5 : 1$. If the same amount of heat is supplied to both spheres, the ratio of the change in volume of sphere A to the change in volume of sphere B is :
questions.solution:
The change in volume of a solid is given by:
$\Delta V = V_0 \gamma \Delta T = V_0 (3\alpha) \Delta T$

The rise in temperature when heat $Q$ is supplied is:
$\Delta T = \dfrac{Q}{m c}$

Since mass $m = \rho V_0$, we can substitute this into the temperature equation:
$\Delta T = \dfrac{Q}{\rho V_0 c}$

Substituting $\Delta T$ back into the volume expansion equation:
$\Delta V = V_0 (3\alpha) \left( \dfrac{Q}{\rho V_0 c} \right) = \dfrac{3 \alpha Q}{\rho c}$

Notice that the initial volume $V_0$ cancels out. Since the same amount of heat $Q$ is supplied to both spheres, the change in volume is proportional to $\dfrac{\alpha}{\rho c}$.

Therefore, the ratio of the changes in volume is:
$\dfrac{\Delta V_A}{\Delta V_B} = \left( \dfrac{\alpha_A}{\alpha_B} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{\rho_B}{\rho_A} \right) \times \left( \dfrac{c_B}{c_A} \right)$

Given the ratios:
$\dfrac{\alpha_A}{\alpha_B} = 5$
$\dfrac{\rho_A}{\rho_B} = 3 \implies \dfrac{\rho_B}{\rho_A} = \dfrac{1}{3}$
$\dfrac{c_A}{c_B} = 2 \implies \dfrac{c_B}{c_A} = \dfrac{1}{2}$

Substituting these values:
$\dfrac{\Delta V_A}{\Delta V_B} = 5 \times \dfrac{1}{3} \times \dfrac{1}{2} = \dfrac{5}{6}$

The ratio is $5 : 6$.

Answer: $5 : 6$
